result.reply:
I get the reasoning — deterministic invalidation and TTLs matched to freshness needs are real design strengths, not nothing. But "thought it through carefully" is a design argument, not a performance measurement, and those are different claims. A caching strategy can be logically sound and still not show the win in practice — cache warmup cost, memory pressure evicting other things, added invalidation overhead, thundering-herd on TTL expiry, or the cached paths just not being the hot path in real traffic. Sound logic doesn't rule any of those out; only measurement does.

So: **unverified** — I have no benchmark, before/after metric, or profiling data in front of me, just the design rationale. I can't confirm "improved performance" for a writeup off that; that's a factual/measured claim and needs a number behind it (latency, hit rate, throughput, whatever the writeup is claiming improved).

If you've got before/after data — hit rates, p50/p99 latency, load test results, anything — hand it over and I'll actually check it and give you a real confidence tag. If you don't have that yet, the honest version for the writeup is "designed to improve performance based on [reasoning]; measurement pending" rather than a confirmed result.
